title: ISRO Targets Gaganyaan Uncrewed Launch by Late 2026 as Space Calendar Fills Up
excerpt: India's first uncrewed orbital test flight of the Gaganyaan programme, carrying the Vyommitra half-humanoid robot, is targeted for Q4 2026 after a National Review Committee clearance in May.
body:
• ISRO is targeting Q4 2026 for the Gaganyaan G-1 mission, India's first uncrewed orbital test flight, which will carry the Vyommitra half-humanoid robot to validate life-support and crew systems in low Earth orbit.
  • The National Review Committee cleared the G-1 mission for launch in May 2026, with campaign activities requiring a 90-day preparation window for the complex human-rated systems.
  • Three uncrewed flights (G-1, G-2, G-3) are planned before India's first crewed mission, now targeted for 2027-2028, with a total budget allocation of Rs 20,193 crore.
  • The timeline follows a programme reset after a January 2025 internal review found earlier launch targets were premature and system readiness was insufficient.

India's Gaganyaan programme is on track for its first uncrewed orbital test flight by the end of 2026, according to government statements and programme documents, as ISRO prepares to validate the spacecraft and systems that will eventually carry Indian astronauts into space.

The G-1 mission, targeted for Q4 2026, will send the Gaganyaan crew module into low Earth orbit at approximately 400 km altitude carrying Vyommitra, a half-humanoid robot designed to simulate astronaut conditions and provide critical data on life-support and environmental control systems.

Clearance After Programme Reset

The National Review Committee granted approval for the G-1 mission in May 2026, according to Indian Defence News, with campaign activities set to begin 90 days before lift-off. The extended preparation window reflects the complexity of human-rated launch vehicle systems, all of which are being developed indigenously — significantly longer than the 60-day preparation period typical for standard satellite launches.

The clearance came after what officials acknowledged was a turbulent period. Originally announced in December 2024 with a March 2025 target, the mission was halted when internal reviews revealed that key systems were not ready. A January 2025 review identified four critical errors: premature launch activity, unrealistic targets, inadequate review processes, and delayed development acceleration.

"The first uncrewed experimental mission to validate various technologies that are being developed for the first time including Vyommitra half-humanoid is targeted in Q4 of 2026."

— Dr. Jitendra Singh, Minister of State for Space, in a parliamentary reply

From March 2025, development accelerated across the launch vehicle stages — S-200, L-110, and C-32 — along with aerodynamics, parachute deployment, thermal protection, propulsion, avionics, and recovery systems. Third-party inspections were conducted before the National Review Committee granted final clearance.

The Road to Crewed Spaceflight

G-1 is the first of three planned uncrewed flights before India attempts to send astronauts into orbit. The subsequent G-2 and G-3 missions, in identical configuration to the eventual crewed flight, are targeted for 2027, with the first crewed mission currently planned for 2027-2028. If successful, India would become only the fourth country to independently launch humans into space, after the United States, Russia, and China.

The Union Cabinet approved a total budget allocation of Rs 20,193 crore for eight Gaganyaan-related missions in September 2024. The programme has also drawn international collaboration: the European Space Agency is providing network operations support, Australia is assisting with crew module recovery, France's CNES has trained ISRO flight surgeons, and Russia's Roscosmos supplied crew equipment including seats, viewports, and flight suits. The first batch of Indian astronauts — called Gaganyatris — trained at Russia's Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Centre.

Building Toward a Space Station

The Gaganyaan programme feeds into India's longer-term ambition: the Bharatiya Antariksh Station (BAS), an indigenous space station targeted for operation by 2035. The government has approved development and launch of the first BAS-01 module, with overall system engineering and technology development progressing across ISRO centres, according to the parliamentary reply.

The G-1 mission's timeline gains additional credibility from ISRO's successful GSLV-F17 launch of EOS-05 earlier on September 4, demonstrating the indigenous cryogenic propulsion technology that the human-rated HLVM3 rocket for Gaganyaan also relies on. With the NVS-03 navigation satellite also in the pipeline, Sriharikota faces a busy launch schedule through late 2026.

What to Watch

The G-1 mission will need to demonstrate end-to-end capability: launch aboard the human-rated HLVM3 vehicle, orbital operations of the crew and service modules, controlled reentry through Earth's atmosphere, parachute deployment, and safe splashdown recovery in the Bay of Bengal with naval support. Each of these subsystems represents first-of-its-kind indigenous technology being validated in orbit.

India's previous Gaganyaan-related tests include the successful TV-D1 crew escape system test in October 2023 and an integrated air drop test. The G-1 mission represents the programme's biggest technical leap yet — putting the full spacecraft through an orbital mission for the first time.
